questions.summary: Compare a line through the origin and the data mean with the least-squares regression line for river depth, then make a prediction.
questions.accessibleText:
1. [Maximum mark: 7]

Kiran and Logan collect the following data about the river Afon, where x is the distance in metres from the source and y is the depth in centimetres.

[Table: Distance from the source x (m): 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 450. Corresponding depth y (cm): 11, 15, 23, 34, 35, 49, 67.]

This data is represented in the following scatter diagram.

[Scatter diagram titled “River Afon”. The horizontal axis is “Distance from source x (m)”, from 0 to 500 with labelled intervals of 100. The vertical axis is “Depth of river y (cm)”, from 0 to 80 with labelled intervals of 10. The seven plotted points are (50, 11), (100, 15), (150, 23), (200, 34), (300, 35), (400, 49) and (450, 67).]

Kiran knows that the depth of the river is 0 cm at the source.

Kiran calculates x̄ and ȳ for the seven points given in the table on page 2 and draws a line on the scatter diagram through the mean point (x̄, ȳ) and the point (0, 0).

(a) Find

(i) the value of x̄ and the value of ȳ;

(ii) the equation of Kiran’s line. [3]

For the seven points given in the table Logan finds the regression line of y on x with equation y = ax + b, where a, b ∈ ℝ.

(b) Determine the value of a and the value of b. [2]

(c) By using the equation of Logan’s regression line, estimate the depth of the river 350 m from its source. [2]
questions.solution: (a)(i) The coordinate means are x̄ = (50 + 100 + 150 + 200 + 300 + 400 + 450)/7 = 1650/7 = 235.714… = 236 m (3 s.f.) and ȳ = (11 + 15 + 23 + 34 + 35 + 49 + 67)/7 = 234/7 = 33.4285… = 33.4 cm (3 s.f.). (ii) Kiran’s line passes through (0, 0) and (x̄, ȳ), so its gradient is ȳ/x̄ = 234/1650 = 0.141818…. Hence y = 0.142x (3 s.f.). (b) For the regression of y on x, a = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)² = 0.125515… and b = ȳ − ax̄ = 3.84278…. Thus a = 0.126 and b = 3.84 (3 s.f.), giving y = 0.125515…x + 3.84278…. (c) At x = 350, y = 0.125515…(350) + 3.84278… = 47.7731…, so the estimated depth is 47.8 cm. These values agree with the official markscheme.

questions.summary: Use bearings to determine two triangle angles and apply the sine rule to find the lighthouse-to-boat distance.
questions.accessibleText:
2. [Maximum mark: 5]

A boat sets off from a port P and travels on a bearing of 090° until reaching point B.

A lighthouse L is 5 km from P on a bearing of 056°.

The bearing of the lighthouse from B is 290°.

This is shown in the following diagram.

[Diagram not to scale: P and B lie on a horizontal east–west line, with B due east of P. A north arrow is drawn at each point. L is above the segment PB, forming triangle PLB. Segment PL is labelled 5 km. At P, the clockwise angle from north to PL is 056°. At B, the clockwise bearing from north to BL is 290°.]

(a) Find the angle LP̂B. [1]

(b) Find LB, the distance from point L to point B. [4]
questions.solution: (a) Since PB has bearing 090° and PL has bearing 056°, angle LP̂B = 090° − 056° = 34°. (b) From B, BP has bearing 270° while BL has bearing 290°, so angle LBP = 290° − 270° = 20°. Therefore angle PLB = 180° − 34° − 20° = 126°. By the sine rule, LB/sin 34° = PL/sin 20° = 5/sin 20°. Hence LB = 5 sin 34°/sin 20° = 8.17485… km = 8.17 km (3 s.f.). These results agree with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Use a double-angle identity to rewrite a trigonometric expression as a quadratic in sin x and solve it on a stated interval.
questions.accessibleText:
3. [Maximum mark: 5]

(a) Show that 3 cos 2x + 11 sin x = 3 + 11 sin x − 6 sin²x. [2]

(b) Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation 3 cos 2x + 11 sin x − 6 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 180°. [3]
questions.solution: (a) Using cos 2x = 1 − 2 sin²x gives 3 cos 2x + 11 sin x = 3(1 − 2 sin²x) + 11 sin x = 3 + 11 sin x − 6 sin²x, as required. (b) Substitute this form into the equation: 3 + 11 sin x − 6 sin²x − 6 = 0, so 6 sin²x − 11 sin x + 3 = 0. Factoring gives (3 sin x − 1)(2 sin x − 3) = 0. Since sin x cannot equal 3/2, sin x = 1/3. On 0° ≤ x ≤ 180°, x = sin⁻¹(1/3) = 19.4712…° or x = 180° − 19.4712…° = 160.528…°. Therefore x = 19.5° or 161° (3 s.f.). These answers agree with the official markscheme.

questions.summary: Reason about how two extreme scores affect a median, then use mean and range information to recover both scores.
questions.accessibleText:
4. [Maximum mark: 6]

A teacher sets her class of 30 pupils a quiz.

Aiden and Brett were absent on the day of the quiz.

The following box and whisker diagram shows the results of the 28 pupils who took the quiz on the day.

[Box and whisker diagram on a quiz-score scale from 6 to 17: minimum 6, lower quartile 6.5, median 10.5, upper quartile 14.5 and maximum 17.]

Aiden and Brett take the quiz when they return.

Aiden scores less than 6.

Brett scores more than 17.

(a) Explain, briefly, why the median score for all 30 pupils would still be 10.5. [1]

The mean score of the 28 pupils was 10.5.

The mean score for all 30 pupils is now 10.6.

The range of scores for all 30 pupils is 14.

(b) Determine Aiden’s score and Brett’s score. [5]
questions.solution: (a) Aiden’s new score lies below every original score and Brett’s lies above every original score. They are therefore added at opposite ends of the ordered list, so the two central original values remain the 15th and 16th values of the 30 scores. Their average, and hence the median, stays 10.5. (b) Let A and B be Aiden’s and Brett’s scores. The original total was 28(10.5) = 294 and the new total is 30(10.6) = 318, so A + B = 24. Because A < 6 and B > 17, they become the new minimum and maximum; the new range gives B − A = 14. Solving the simultaneous equations, 2B = 38, so B = 19 and A = 5. Thus Aiden scored 5 and Brett scored 19, agreeing with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Relate the perimeter and area of a circle and a sector, then solve for the sector’s acute central angle.
questions.accessibleText:
5. [Maximum mark: 6]

Consider a circle and a sector.

The radius of the circle is 8 mm.

The radius of the sector is r mm and the acute angle at the centre is θ radians.

This is shown in the following diagram.

[Diagram not to scale: A circle with a radius marked 8 is shown beside a separate circular sector. The sector has radius r and acute central angle θ.]

The perimeter of the sector is 1.5 times the circumference of the circle.

(a) Show that r = 24π/(2 + θ). [3]

It is given that the area of the circle is the same as the area of the sector.

(b) Determine the value of θ. [3]
questions.solution: (a) The circle’s circumference is 2π(8) = 16π mm, so the sector’s perimeter is 1.5(16π) = 24π mm. A sector of radius r and angle θ has perimeter 2r + rθ = r(2 + θ). Thus r(2 + θ) = 24π and r = 24π/(2 + θ), as required. (b) Equality of areas gives 64π = ½r²θ. Substituting the expression for r, 64π = ½[24π/(2 + θ)]²θ. After simplification, (2 + θ)² = (9π/2)θ, or θ² + (4 − 9π/2)θ + 4 = 0. Solving gives θ = 0.411273… or θ = 9.72589…. Since θ is acute, 0 < θ < π/2, so θ = 0.411 radians (3 s.f.). This agrees with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Use normal-distribution quantiles for two related sunflower populations to determine a standardized constant, mean and standard deviation.
questions.accessibleText:
6. [Maximum mark: 7]

A garden centre sells seeds for two varieties of sunflowers: large and giant.

The heights of large sunflowers are normally distributed with mean m and standard deviation s.

It is known that 25% of large sunflowers have a height of over 180 cm.

(a) Given that m + As = 180, where A ∈ ℝ, find the value of A. [3]

The heights of giant sunflowers are also normally distributed.

The giant sunflowers have a mean height that is 35 cm more than that of the large sunflowers and a standard deviation that is double that of the large sunflowers.

It is known that 98% of giant sunflowers have a height greater than 180 cm.

(b) Determine m and s. [4]
questions.solution: Let X be a large-sunflower height, so X ~ N(m, s²). Since P(X > 180) = 0.25, P(X ≤ 180) = 0.75 and (180 − m)/s = Φ⁻¹(0.75) = 0.674489…. Therefore m + 0.674489…s = 180, so (a) A = 0.674 (3 s.f.). For giant sunflowers, let Y ~ N(m + 35, (2s)²). Since P(Y > 180) = 0.98, P(Y ≤ 180) = 0.02, so [180 − (m + 35)]/(2s) = Φ⁻¹(0.02) = −2.053748…. Hence 145 − m = −4.107497…s, or m = 145 + 4.107497…s. Combining this with m = 180 − 0.674489…s gives 35 = 4.781987…s, so s = 7.31913… and m = 175.063…. Thus m = 175 cm and s = 7.32 cm (3 s.f.), agreeing with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Compare simple monthly interest based on the initial principal with annual compound interest and find when the compound account overtakes.
questions.accessibleText:
7. [Maximum mark: 12]

Andy and Jess each have $5000.

Andy invests the money in a new savings plan that will pay interest at the end of each month.

Andy will receive a fixed amount of interest each month. The amount received is 0.315% of the initial investment.

(a) (i) Determine the amount of interest Andy will receive at the end of each month. Give this answer correct to two decimal places.

(ii) Hence, determine the amount of interest Andy will receive each year.

(iii) Write down an expression in the form 5000 + pn, where p ∈ ℤ⁺, for the amount of money Andy will have in his savings plan at the end of n years.

(iv) Hence, show that Andy will have $5945 in his savings plan at the end of 5 years. [4]

In this part, where appropriate, give all answers to the nearest dollar.

Jess invests her $5000 in a new account that pays 3% interest compounded annually.

(b) (i) Determine the amount of money that will be in Jess’s account at the end of 5 years.

(ii) Hence, find the amount of interest Jess will receive in the 5 years. [3]

(c) (i) Write an expression in the form 5000 × qⁿ, where q ∈ ℝ⁺, for the amount of money that Jess will have in her account at the end of n years.

(ii) Hence, determine the smallest number of complete years that it will take for Jess to have more money in her account than Andy has in his savings plan. [5]
questions.solution: (a)(i) Andy’s monthly interest is 0.315% of $5000: 5000(0.00315) = $15.75. (ii) In one year he receives 12(15.75) = $189. (iii) After n years his balance is 5000 + 189n, so p = 189. (iv) At n = 5, 5000 + 189(5) = 5000 + 945 = $5945, as required. (b)(i) Jess’s balance after 5 years is 5000(1.03)⁵ = $5796.370…, which is $5796 to the nearest dollar. (ii) Her interest is 5796.370… − 5000 = $796.370…, or $796 to the nearest dollar. (c)(i) Jess’s balance after n years is 5000(1.03)ⁿ, so q = 1.03. (ii) We need 5000(1.03)ⁿ > 5000 + 189n. Numerical solution of the equality gives n = 16.0097…, so the first complete integer year after the crossing is n = 17. Indeed, at n = 16 Jess has $8023.53 while Andy has $8024, but at n = 17 Jess has $8264.24 while Andy has $8213. Therefore the smallest number is 17 years. All results agree with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Calculate a hemisphere-and-cone model’s volume and cone surface area, derive a fixed-volume constraint, and minimize the coating area.
questions.accessibleText:
8. [Maximum mark: 15]

A manufacturer creates an ice cream model consisting of two parts.

The top part consists of a hemisphere of ice cream with radius r cm.

The bottom part consists of a cone of ice cream with radius r cm and height h cm, which is wrapped in a wafer coating.

This is shown in the following diagram.

[Diagram: A hemisphere and an inverted cone are shown separately with a plus sign, then combined into an ice cream model. The hemisphere sits on the cone’s circular top. Both have radius r; the cone has vertical height h. The cone’s curved exterior is labelled “wafer coating”.]

(a) Consider the case where r = 3 and h = 8.

(i) Show that the total volume, V, of ice cream is 132 cm³, correct to 3 significant figures.

(ii) Determine the curved surface area, S, of the wafer coating. [7]

The manufacturer changes the dimensions of the model to ensure that the total volume, V, of ice cream is 120 cm³.

(b) Show that h = (360 − 2πr³)/(πr²). [3]

(c) Hence, show that the curved surface area of the wafer coating is given by

S = πr√(r² + ((360 − 2πr³)/(πr²))²). [2]

The manufacturer wants to use the minimum possible value of S.

(d) Determine the minimum value of S and the corresponding value of r. [3]
questions.solution: (a)(i) With r = 3 and h = 8, V = (2/3)πr³ + (1/3)πr²h = (2/3)π(27) + (1/3)π(9)(8) = 18π + 24π = 42π = 131.946… cm³ = 132 cm³ (3 s.f.). (ii) The cone’s slant height is l = √(r² + h²) = √(3² + 8²) = √73. Its curved surface area is S = πrl = 3π√73 = 80.5253… cm² = 80.5 cm². (b) For the redesigned model, (2/3)πr³ + (1/3)πr²h = 120. Multiplying by 3 and rearranging gives πr²h = 360 − 2πr³, hence h = (360 − 2πr³)/(πr²). (c) Since l = √(r² + h²) and S = πrl, substitution of the expression for h gives S = πr√(r² + ((360 − 2πr³)/(πr²))²), as required. (d) For r > 0 with h > 0, minimize this one-variable function using a GDC or by solving dS/dr = 0. The minimum occurs at r = 3.67084… cm, where h = 1.16228… cm and S = 44.4045… cm². Thus the minimum coating area is 44.4 cm² and the corresponding radius is 3.67 cm (3 s.f.). These results agree with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Analyse damped sinusoidal displacement for extrema, velocity and distance, then use its geometric decay to find an infinite travel distance.
questions.accessibleText:
9. [Maximum mark: 17]

A particle P moves in a straight line so that its displacement, s cm, from a fixed point O at time t seconds is given by s(t) = 2^(1 − t/5) sin(2πt/3), where t ≥ 0.

The following diagram shows part of the graph of y = s(t).

[Graph: A damped sinusoidal curve on axes labelled s(t) vertically and t horizontally. It begins at the origin with positive slope, then oscillates above and below the t-axis with steadily decreasing amplitude.]

(a) Find

(i) the maximum displacement of P from O;

(ii) the maximum velocity of P. [5]

(b) Find

(i) the minimum value of the displacement function s(t);

(ii) the displacement of P from O when t = 3.5. [3]

(c) Hence, determine the total distance travelled by P in the first 3.5 seconds. [3]

The first time that P returns and passes through O is when t = T.

(d) Write down the value of T. [1]

The particle passes through O every T seconds.

A sequence u₁, u₂, u₃ … is formed where u₁, u₂, u₃ … are the largest distances from O in each of the intervals 0 < t < T, T < t < 2T, 2T < t < 3T … respectively.

It is known that u₁, u₂, u₃ … form a geometric sequence.

(e) (i) Determine the value of the common ratio r of this geometric sequence.

(ii) Calculate the total distance travelled by the particle if it were to continue to move in this way indefinitely. [5]
questions.solution: Write s(t) = 2e^(−kt)sin(ωt), where k = ln 2/5 and ω = 2π/3. Then v(t) = s′(t) = 2e^(−kt)[ω cos(ωt) − k sin(ωt)]. (a)(i) At a nonzero stationary point, tan(ωt) = ω/k. The first positive maximum occurs at t = 0.718442… and gives s = 1.80645… cm, so the maximum displacement is 1.81 cm. Later maxima are smaller because of the factor 2^(−t/5). (ii) The greatest positive velocity occurs at t = 0; v(0) = 2ω = 4π/3 = 4.18879… cm s⁻¹, so the maximum velocity is 4.19 cm s⁻¹. (b)(i) The first minimum occurs at t = 0.718442… + 1.5 = 2.218442… and gives s = −1.46729… cm, so the minimum value is −1.47 cm. (ii) s(3.5) = 2^(1 − 3.5/5)sin(7π/3) = 1.06620… cm = 1.07 cm. (c) From t = 0 to 3.5, the particle travels from 0 to the first maximum, back through 0 to the first minimum, back through 0 to the second maximum, then back to s(3.5). Equivalently, the successive turning values needed are 1.80645…, −1.46729…, 1.19181… and s(3.5) = 1.06620…. The distance is 1.80645 + (1.80645 + 1.46729) + (1.46729 + 1.19181) + (1.19181 − 1.06620) = 7.61369… cm, so 7.61 cm. (d) Zeros occur when sin(2πt/3) = 0, so the first positive zero is T = 3/2 = 1.5 seconds. (e)(i) Each interval is T = 1.5 seconds later than the previous one. The sinusoidal shape repeats in absolute value, while the amplitude is multiplied by 2^(−T/5). Therefore r = 2^(−1.5/5) = 2^(−3/10) = 0.812252… = 0.812. (ii) In each interval between consecutive crossings of O, the particle travels from O to its largest distance uₙ and back to O, a distance 2uₙ. Since u₁ = 1.80645… and the uₙ form a geometric sequence, total distance = 2[u₁/(1 − r)] = 2(1.80645…)/(1 − 0.812252…) = 19.2433… cm = 19.2 cm. These values agree with the official markscheme.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

The second term of an arithmetic sequence is 10 and the fourth term is 22.

(a) Find the value of the common difference. [2]

(b) Find an expression for uₙ, the nth term. [2]
questions.solution: u₄−u₂=2d=12, so d=6. Then u₁=10−6=4 and uₙ=4+6(n−1)=6n−2.

questions.summary: Find missing frequencies and transform a mean.
questions.accessibleText:
2. [Maximum mark: 6]

Claire rolls a six-sided die 16 times. The scores are shown in the frequency table.

[Table: Score 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; frequency p, q, 4, 2, 0, 3 respectively.]

The mean score is 3.

questions.summary: Grouped statistics, binomial and conditional probability.
questions.accessibleText:
7. [Maximum mark: 14]

MyLife is a social media platform with 89.8 million users, all aged 12 years old and above. The following frequency table shows the number of users by age group.

| Age, a (years) | Millions of users |
|---|---:|
| 12 ≤ a < 18 | 5.8 |
| 18 ≤ a < 35 | 42.7 |
| 35 ≤ a < 55 | 26.3 |
| 55 ≤ a < 75 | 12.9 |
| 75 ≤ a < 95 | 2.1 |
| Total | 89.8 |

(a) Find the percentage of MyLife users aged 55 years or older. [1]

(b) A sample of 1000 MyLife users is chosen at random. Find the probability that fewer than 150 of them are aged 55 years or older. [3]

(c) Given that a MyLife user chosen at random is 55 years or older, find the probability that they are 75 years or older. [4]

(d) List the mid-interval value for each class interval. [1]

(e) Hence, for MyLife users, estimate
(i) the mean age;
(ii) the variance of the ages. [3]

A different social media platform, SmallTalk, reports that its users have a mean age of 29.9 years and a variance of 137 years². The following four diagrams represent age distributions.

[Diagrams A–D each show a solid and a dotted bell-shaped age-distribution curve. A: both curves have the same centre; the dotted curve is narrower and taller than the solid curve. B: the dotted curve is centred to the right of the solid curve and is narrower and taller. C: the solid curve is centred to the right of the dotted curve and is narrower and taller. D: the dotted curve is centred to the left of the solid curve and is narrower and taller; the solid curve is wider and lower.]

(f) (i) Identify the diagram which best represents the age distributions for the users of MyLife and SmallTalk.
(ii) In your chosen diagram, identify which social media platform is represented by the dotted line. [2]
questions.solution:
(a) The number aged at least 55 is 12.9 + 2.1 = 15.0 million, so the percentage is (15.0/89.8) × 100 = 16.7037…% ≈ 16.7%.

(b) For a randomly selected user, p = 15.0/89.8 = 0.167037…. Let X be the number aged at least 55 in a random sample of 1000. Then X ~ B(1000, 15.0/89.8), and “fewer than 150” means X ≤ 149. Hence
P(X < 150) = P(X ≤ 149) = Σ(x=0 to 149) C(1000,x)pˣ(1−p)¹⁰⁰⁰⁻ˣ = 0.0669378… ≈ 0.0669.

(c) In context,
P(age ≥ 75 | age ≥ 55) = P(age ≥ 75)/P(age ≥ 55)
= 2.1/(12.9 + 2.1) = 2.1/15.0 = 0.14 (= 7/50).

(d) Each midpoint is the average of the class endpoints: (12+18)/2 = 15, (18+35)/2 = 26.5, (35+55)/2 = 45, (55+75)/2 = 65, (75+95)/2 = 85. Thus the mid-interval values are 15, 26.5, 45, 65, 85.

(e) Use the class midpoints as representative ages.
(i) Estimated mean
= [5.8(15) + 42.7(26.5) + 26.3(45) + 12.9(65) + 2.1(85)]/89.8
= 38.0740… ≈ 38.1 years.
(ii) First calculate E(a²):
E(a²) = [5.8(15²) + 42.7(26.5²) + 26.3(45²) + 12.9(65²) + 2.1(85²)]/89.8
= 1717.4117…. Therefore
Var(a) = E(a²) − [E(a)]² = 1717.4117… − (38.0740…)² = 267.778… ≈ 268 years².

(f) MyLife has the larger mean (38.1 > 29.9), so its curve must be centred farther right. It also has the larger variance (268 > 137), so its curve must be wider and lower. This is diagram D. The narrower, left-centred dotted curve therefore represents SmallTalk.
questions.solutionStatus: Independent worked solutions — checked against the official IB markscheme

questions.summary: Compare regression, exponential, and logistic models.
questions.accessibleText:
8. [Maximum mark: 15]

The following table shows the population of Canada t years after the year 2000.

| t (years after 2000) | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| p (population in millions) | 30.6 | 32.3 | 34.1 | 35.6 | 38.0 |

A student uses linear regression to model the population of Canada using these data. The student model is p = at + b.

(a) (i) Write down the value of a and the value of b.
(ii) Interpret, in context, the value of a. [3]

The student uses this model to predict the population of Canada in the year 2030, where t = 30, and calculates a population of approximately 41.4 million people.

(b) Comment on the reliability of the student’s prediction. [1]

A data scientist, Benoit, uses additional information to develop an exponential model for Canada’s future population. In this model, B(t) = 30.6(1.007)ᵗ represents the millions of people in Canada t years after the year 2000, where 25 ≤ t ≤ 100.

(c) (i) Use Benoit’s model to predict the population of Canada in the year 2100.
(ii) Interpret, in context, the value 1.007 in Benoit’s model. [3]

Another data scientist, Cecilia, develops a third model for the Canadian population. In this model, C(t) = 61/(1 + e⁻⁰·⁰³ᵗ) represents the millions of people in Canada t years after the year 2000, where 25 ≤ t ≤ 100.

(d) Use Cecilia’s model to predict the population of Canada in the year 2100. [1]

(e) Determine the year in which the difference between the predictions from Benoit’s model and Cecilia’s model is greatest. [3]

(f) Find the value of
(i) B′(40);
(ii) C′(40). [2]

(g) Compare and interpret, in context, the values of B′(40) and C′(40). [2]
questions.solution:
(a) (i) Linear regression of p on t gives p = 0.362t + 30.5, so a = 0.362 and b = 30.5. (Indeed, at t = 30 this gives p = 0.362(30) + 30.5 = 41.36 ≈ 41.4 million.)
(ii) The slope means that this model predicts an average increase of 0.362 million people per year (about 362 000 people per year).

(b) The 2030 value uses t = 30, outside the observed interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 20. It is an extrapolation, so it is unreliable/uncertain because the past linear trend may not continue.

(c) (i) The year 2100 corresponds to t = 100. Thus B(100) = 30.6(1.007)¹⁰⁰ = 61.4707… ≈ 61.5 million people.
(ii) The factor 1.007 means that Benoit’s model increases the population by 0.7% each year.

(d) C(100) = 61/(1 + e⁻³) = 58.1070… ≈ 58.1 million people.

(e) Let D(t) = C(t) − B(t) on 25 ≤ t ≤ 100. A numerical maximum of D (equivalently, solve D′(t) = C′(t) − B′(t) = 0 and compare with the endpoints) occurs at t = 45.9583…. Since t is years after 2000, the required year is 2045 (2046 is also consistent with rounding to the nearest whole year).

(f) B′(t) = 30.6(1.007)ᵗ ln(1.007), so B′(40) = 0.282151… ≈ 0.282 million people per year. Also
C′(t) = [61(0.03)e⁻⁰·⁰³ᵗ]/(1 + e⁻⁰·⁰³ᵗ)²,
so C′(40) = 0.325546… ≈ 0.326 million people per year.

(g) Since B′(40) < C′(40), Cecilia’s model predicts that in 2040 Canada’s population is increasing faster than Benoit’s model predicts (by about 0.0434 million people per year).

9. [Maximum mark: 16]

In this question all values of x and t are in radians.

Consider the function f(x) = 3 sin(4πx).

(a) (i) Write down the amplitude of the graph of f.
(ii) Find the period of f. [3]

Consider a second function g(x) = −4 cos(4πx). The sum of these functions can be expressed in the form f(x) + g(x) = a cos(b(x − c)), where a, b, c > 0.

(b) By considering the graph of y = f(x) + g(x), determine
(i) the value of a;
(ii) the value of b;
(iii) the smallest possible value of c. [4]

A car is travelling along a straight residential street with speed bumps placed at regular intervals on the road to encourage safer driving. The car travels at a minimum velocity when passing over speed bumps and reaches a maximum velocity in between speed bumps. Its velocity, in m s⁻¹, can be modelled by the function v(t) = −3.5 cos((π/14)(t − 5)) + 9, where t is measured in seconds.

(c) Find the time at which the car first reaches its maximum velocity. [1]

(d) Find the number of speed bumps the car passes over in the first two minutes of motion. [1]

(e) (i) Find v′(t).
(ii) Hence, or otherwise, write down the maximum acceleration of the car. [4]

(f) Find the distance, in metres, between consecutive speed bumps. [3]
questions.solution:
(a) (i) For f(x) = 3 sin(4πx), the amplitude is |3| = 3.
(ii) The period is 2π/(4π) = 1/2.

(b) Let θ = 4πx. Write 3 sin θ − 4 cos θ = R cos(θ − φ) = R cos θ cos φ + R sin θ sin φ. Matching coefficients gives R cos φ = −4 and R sin φ = 3. Hence R = √(4² + 3²) = 5, so a = 5, and b = 4π. The angle φ is in quadrant II, with φ = π − arctan(3/4) = 2.49809…. Since bc = φ, the smallest positive c is φ/(4π) = 0.198792… ≈ 0.199.

(c) The velocity is maximal when cos((π/14)(t − 5)) = −1. The first non-negative solution satisfies (π/14)(t − 5) = π, giving t = 19 seconds.

(d) Velocity minima, and hence speed bumps, occur when cos((π/14)(t − 5)) = 1: t = 5 + 28k. In 0 ≤ t ≤ 120 these are t = 5, 33, 61, 89, 117, so the car passes 5 speed bumps.

(e) (i) By the chain rule,
v′(t) = 3.5(π/14) sin((π/14)(t − 5)) = (π/4) sin((π/14)(t − 5)).
(ii) Acceleration is v′(t). Since the maximum value of sine is 1, the maximum acceleration is π/4 = 0.785398… ≈ 0.785 m s⁻².

(f) Consecutive minima are one period apart, and the period is 2π/(π/14) = 28 seconds. The distance is the integral of velocity over any one period, for example
∫(from 5 to 33) [−3.5 cos((π/14)(t − 5)) + 9] dt.
The cosine term integrates to zero over a full period, so the distance is 9(28) = 252 m.

questions.summary: Grouped statistics, binomial and conditional probability.
questions.accessibleText:
7. [Maximum mark: 14]

MyLife is a social media platform with 93.6 million users, all aged 13 years old and above. The following frequency table shows the number of users by age group.

| Age, a (years) | Millions of users |
|---|---:|
| 13 ≤ a < 18 | 5.5 |
| 18 ≤ a < 25 | 23.6 |
| 25 ≤ a < 45 | 43.5 |
| 45 ≤ a < 65 | 17.3 |
| 65 ≤ a < 85 | 3.7 |
| Total | 93.6 |

(a) Find the percentage of MyLife users aged 45 years or older. [1]

(b) A sample of 1000 MyLife users is chosen at random. Find the probability that fewer than 200 of them are aged 45 years or older. [3]

(c) Given that a MyLife user chosen at random is 45 years or older, find the probability that they are 65 years or older. [4]

(d) List the mid-interval value for each class interval. [1]

(e) Hence, for MyLife users, estimate
(i) the mean age;
(ii) the variance of the ages. [3]

A different social media platform, SmallTalk, reports that its users have a mean age of 29.9 years and a variance of 137 years². The following four diagrams represent age distributions.

[Diagrams A–D each show a solid and a dotted bell-shaped age-distribution curve. A: the solid curve is centred to the left and is wider and lower; the dotted curve is centred to the right and is narrower and taller. B: both curves have the same centre; the dotted curve is narrower and taller than the solid curve. C: the dotted curve is centred to the left and is narrower and taller; the solid curve is centred to the right and is wider and lower. D: the dotted curve is centred to the left and is wider and lower; the solid curve is centred to the right and is narrower and taller.]

(f) (i) Identify the diagram which best represents the age distributions for the users of MyLife and SmallTalk.
(ii) In your chosen diagram, identify which social media platform is represented by the solid line. [2]
questions.solution:
(a) The number aged at least 45 is 17.3 + 3.7 = 21.0 million, so the percentage is (21.0/93.6) × 100 = 22.4359…% ≈ 22.4%.

(b) For a randomly selected user, p = 21.0/93.6 = 0.224359…. Let X be the number aged at least 45 in a random sample of 1000. Then X ~ B(1000, 21.0/93.6), and “fewer than 200” means X ≤ 199. Hence
P(X < 200) = P(X ≤ 199) = Σ(x=0 to 199) C(1000,x)pˣ(1−p)¹⁰⁰⁰⁻ˣ = 0.0284945… ≈ 0.0285.

(c) In context,
P(age ≥ 65 | age ≥ 45) = P(age ≥ 65)/P(age ≥ 45)
= 3.7/(17.3 + 3.7) = 3.7/21.0 = 0.176190… ≈ 0.176 (= 37/210).

(d) Each midpoint is the average of the class endpoints: (13+18)/2 = 15.5, (18+25)/2 = 21.5, (25+45)/2 = 35, (45+65)/2 = 55, (65+85)/2 = 75. Thus the mid-interval values are 15.5, 21.5, 35, 55, 75.

(e) Use the class midpoints as representative ages.
(i) Estimated mean
= [5.5(15.5) + 23.6(21.5) + 43.5(35) + 17.3(55) + 3.7(75)]/93.6
= 35.7281… ≈ 35.7 years.
(ii) First calculate E(a²):
E(a²) = [5.5(15.5²) + 23.6(21.5²) + 43.5(35²) + 17.3(55²) + 3.7(75²)]/93.6
= 1481.4420…. Therefore
Var(a) = E(a²) − [E(a)]² = 1481.4420… − (35.7281…)² = 204.945… ≈ 205 years².

(f) MyLife has the larger mean (35.7 > 29.9), so its curve must be centred farther right. It also has the larger variance (205 > 137), so its curve must be wider and lower. This is diagram C. The right-centred, wider solid curve therefore represents MyLife.

questions.accessibleText:
8. [Maximum mark: 15]

The following table shows the population of Canada t years after the year 2000.

| t (years after 2000) | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| p (population in millions) | 30.7 | 32.2 | 34.0 | 35.7 | 37.9 |

A student uses linear regression to model the population of Canada using these data. The student model is p = at + b.

(a) (i) Write down the value of a and the value of b.
(ii) Interpret, in context, the value of a. [3]

The student uses this model to predict the population of Canada in the year 2030, where t = 30, and calculates a population of approximately 41.3 million people.

(b) Comment on the reliability of the student’s prediction. [1]

A data scientist, Benoit, uses additional information to develop an exponential model for Canada’s future population. In this model, B(t) = 33.5(1.005)ᵗ represents the millions of people in Canada t years after the year 2000, where 25 ≤ t ≤ 100.

(c) (i) Use Benoit’s model to predict the population of Canada in the year 2100.
(ii) Interpret, in context, the value 1.005 in Benoit’s model. [3]

Another data scientist, Cecilia, develops a third model for the Canadian population. In this model, C(t) = 62/(1 + e⁻⁰·⁰²ᵗ) represents the millions of people in Canada t years after the year 2000, where 25 ≤ t ≤ 100.

(d) Use Cecilia’s model to predict the population of Canada in the year 2100. [1]

(e) Determine the year in which the difference between the predictions from Benoit’s model and Cecilia’s model is greatest. [3]

(f) Find the value of
(i) B′(75);
(ii) C′(75). [2]

(g) Compare and interpret, in context, the values of B′(75) and C′(75). [2]
questions.solution:
(a) (i) Linear regression of p on t gives p = 0.358t + 30.52, so a = 0.358 and b = 30.52 (b ≈ 30.5 to 3 s.f.). At t = 30 this gives p = 0.358(30) + 30.52 = 41.26 ≈ 41.3 million.
(ii) The slope means that this model predicts an average increase of 0.358 million people per year (about 358 000 people per year).

(b) The 2030 value uses t = 30, outside the observed interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 20. It is an extrapolation, so it is unreliable/uncertain because the past linear trend may not continue.

(c) (i) The year 2100 corresponds to t = 100. Thus B(100) = 33.5(1.005)¹⁰⁰ = 55.1633… ≈ 55.2 million people.
(ii) The factor 1.005 means that Benoit’s model increases the population by 0.5% each year.

(d) C(100) = 62/(1 + e⁻²) = 54.6094… ≈ 54.6 million people.

(e) Let D(t) = C(t) − B(t) on 25 ≤ t ≤ 100. A numerical maximum of D (equivalently, solve D′(t) = C′(t) − B′(t) = 0 and compare with the endpoints) occurs at t = 58.6283…. Since t is years after 2000, the required year is 2058 (2059 is also consistent with rounding to the nearest whole year).

(f) B′(t) = 33.5(1.005)ᵗ ln(1.005), so B′(75) = 0.242876… ≈ 0.243 million people per year. Also
C′(t) = [62(0.02)e⁻⁰·⁰²ᵗ]/(1 + e⁻⁰·⁰²ᵗ)²,
so C′(75) = 0.184941… ≈ 0.185 million people per year.

(g) Since B′(75) > C′(75), Benoit’s model predicts that in 2075 Canada’s population is increasing faster than Cecilia’s model predicts (by about 0.0579 million people per year).

(b) By considering the graph of y = f(x) + g(x), determine
(i) the value of a;
(ii) the value of b;
(iii) the smallest possible value of c. [4]

A car is travelling along a straight residential street with speed bumps placed at regular intervals on the road to encourage safer driving. The car travels at a minimum velocity when passing over speed bumps and reaches a maximum velocity in between speed bumps. Its velocity, in m s⁻¹, can be modelled by the function v(t) = −4.5 cos((π/19)(t − 4)) + 10.5, where t is measured in seconds.

(c) Find the time at which the car first reaches its maximum velocity. [1]

(d) Find the number of speed bumps the car passes over in the first two minutes of motion. [1]

(e) (i) Find v′(t).
(ii) Hence, or otherwise, write down the maximum acceleration of the car. [4]

questions.solution:
(a) (i) For f(x) = 6 cos(πx), the amplitude is |6| = 6.
(ii) The period is 2π/π = 2.

(b) Let θ = πx. Write 6 cos θ − 8 sin θ = R cos(θ − φ) = R cos θ cos φ + R sin θ sin φ. Matching coefficients gives R cos φ = 6 and R sin φ = −8. Hence R = √(6² + 8²) = 10, so a = 10, and b = π. For the smallest positive phase in this form, take φ = 2π − arctan(4/3) = 5.35589…. Since bc = φ, the smallest positive c is φ/π = 1.70483… ≈ 1.70.

(c) The velocity is maximal when cos((π/19)(t − 4)) = −1. The first non-negative solution satisfies (π/19)(t − 4) = π, giving t = 23 seconds.

(d) Velocity minima, and hence speed bumps, occur when cos((π/19)(t − 4)) = 1: t = 4 + 38k. In 0 ≤ t ≤ 120 these are t = 4, 42, 80, 118, so the car passes 4 speed bumps.

(e) (i) By the chain rule,

(ii) Acceleration is v′(t). Since the maximum value of sine is 1, the maximum acceleration is 9π/38 = 0.744061… ≈ 0.744 m s⁻².

(f) Consecutive minima are one period apart, and the period is 2π/(π/19) = 38 seconds. The distance is the integral of velocity over any one period, for example

9. [Maximum mark: 17]

An object moves along a straight line. Its velocity, v m s⁻¹, at time t seconds is given by v(t) = −t³ + (7/2)t² − 2t + 6, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. The object first comes to rest at t = k.

[Graph: v starts positive at t=0, decreases to a local minimum, rises to a local maximum, then decreases through the t-axis at t=k and becomes negative.]

At t = 0, the object is at the origin.

(a) Find the displacement of the object from the origin at t = 1. [5]

(b) Find an expression for the acceleration of the object. [2]

(c) Hence, find the greatest speed reached by the object before it comes to rest. [5]

(d) Find the greatest speed reached by the object for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. [2]

(e) Write down an expression that represents the distance travelled by the object while its speed is increasing. Do not evaluate the expression. [3]
questions.solution: (a) Displacement is ∫₀¹v(t)dt=[−t⁴/4+7t³/6−t²+6t]₀¹=71/12 m. (b) a(t)=v′(t)=−3t²+7t−2. (c) a=0 gives (3t−1)(t−2)=0, so t=1/3 or 2. Before the first rest, the greatest velocity occurs at t=2 and v(2)=8; greatest speed is 8 m s⁻¹. (d) Also check t=4: v(4)=−10, so the greatest speed on [0,4] is 10 m s⁻¹. (e) Speed increases on [1/3,2] and [k,4], so one expression is ∫_(1/3)^2 v(t)dt − ∫_k^4 v(t)dt.

The functions f and g are defined for x ∈ ℝ by

f(x) = ax + b, where a, b ∈ ℤ,
g(x) = x² + x + 3.

Find the two possible functions f such that (g ∘ f)(x) = 4x² − 14x + 15.

[Diagram: an upward-opening parabola with vertex (−2,−5), crossing the y-axis at P.]

[Diagram: the normal L passes through P and intersects the parabola again at Q.]

A circle with equation x² + y² = 9 has centre (0, 0) and radius 3. A triangle, PQR, is inscribed in the circle with its vertices at P(−3, 0), Q(x, y) and R(x, −y), where Q and R are variable points in the first and fourth quadrants respectively.

[Diagram: P is the leftmost point of the circle; Q and R are vertically aligned on the right, forming triangle PQR.]

(a) For point Q, show that y = √(9 − x²). [1]

(b) Hence, find an expression for A, the area of triangle PQR, in terms of x. [3]

(c) Show that dA/dx = (9 − 3x − 2x²)/√(9 − x²). [4]

(d) Hence or otherwise, find the y-coordinate of R such that A is a maximum. [6]
questions.solution: (a) Since Q lies on x²+y²=9 and y>0, y=√(9−x²). (b) Base QR=2y and perpendicular height from P is x+3, so A=(1/2)(2√(9−x²))(x+3)=(x+3)√(9−x²). (c) Product and chain rules give A′=√(9−x²)−x(x+3)/√(9−x²)=(9−3x−2x²)/√(9−x²). (d) Set the numerator to zero: 2x²+3x−9=(2x−3)(x+3)=0. In the first quadrant x=3/2. Point R has y-coordinate −√(9−9/4)=−3√3/2.

An engineer is designing a gutter to catch rainwater from the roof of a house. The gutter will be open at the top and is made by folding a piece of sheet metal 45 cm wide and 600 cm long.

[Diagram not to scale: rectangular sheet metal, 600 cm by 45 cm.]

[Diagram: a weight suspended from a spring above the ground.]

The weight is released at a minimum height of 1 m and reaches a maximum of 1.8 m.

[Graph: H oscillates between 1 and 1.8 over 0≤t≤10, starting at H=1.]

A ballet company performs The Sleeping Beauty every year. Last year they gave a total of 60 performances at their theatre which has a maximum capacity of 800. The number of tickets sold, n, at each performance is shown in the following frequency table.

[Table: Number of tickets sold, n | Number of performances; 0 < n ≤ 200 | 3; 200 < n ≤ 400 | p; 400 < n ≤ 600 | 18; 600 < n ≤ 800 | 30.]

(a) (i) Find the value of p.
    (ii) Write down the modal class. [2]

The following cumulative frequency diagram also displays these data.

[Diagram: Cumulative frequency curve with number of tickets sold from 0 to 800 on the horizontal axis and cumulative frequency from 0 to 60 on the vertical axis. The curve passes through approximately (0, 0), (200, 3), (400, 12), (600, 30) and (800, 60).]

(b) Use the cumulative frequency curve to estimate
    (i) the median number of tickets sold;
    (ii) the number of performances where at least 80% of the tickets were sold. [4]

After a performance, the company decides to conduct a survey to obtain feedback from the audience.

(c) (i) State one disadvantage of the company surveying only the first 5% of the audience as they leave the theatre.
    (ii) Describe briefly how the company could collect feedback from 5% of the audience using the systematic sampling method.
    (iii) State the sampling method which should be used if the survey is to be representative of the number of children and the number of adults in the audience. [4]

Last year 36 000 tickets were sold to The Sleeping Beauty.

(d) The following box and whisker diagram displays the amount spent by the audience at the souvenir shop when they attended the performance.

[Diagram: Horizontal box plot of Amount Spent ($), with minimum 0, lower quartile 3, median 7, upper quartile 13 and maximum 25.]

    (i) Estimate the number of people who spent between $3 and $25.
    (ii) Half the audience spent less than $a. Estimate the value of a. [3]

(e) This year the company will again give 60 performances and expects to sell 18 additional tickets for each performance.
    (i) Calculate the mean number of tickets the company expects to sell this year for each performance.
    (ii) State what effect, if any, this increase in ticket sales would have on the variance of the number of tickets sold for each performance. [4]
questions.solution: (a)(i) p = 60 − 3 − 18 − 30 = 9. (ii) The modal class is 600 < n ≤ 800. (b)(i) The median is read at cumulative frequency 30, giving about 600 tickets. (ii) 80% of 800 is 640 tickets. The curve gives about 40 performances below 640, so about 60 − 40 = 20 performances sold at least 80%. (c)(i) The first 5% is a convenience sample and may be biased, for example because those people may leave from the same seating area or group. (ii) Choose a random starting person among the first 20, then survey every 20th person, since 5% = 1/20. (iii) Use quota sampling for children and adults. (d)(i) From Q₁ = $3 to the maximum $25 contains 75% of the audience, so 0.75(36 000) = 27 000 people. (ii) The median is $7, so a = 7. Let f(x) = −2x + 3, for x ∈ ℝ.

(a) The graph of a linear function g is parallel to the graph of f and passes through the origin. Find an expression for g(x). [2]

(b) The graph of a linear function h is perpendicular to the graph of f and passes through the point (−1, 2). Find an expression for h(x). [3]

(c) Find (g ∘ h)(0). [2]
questions.solution: (a) A parallel line has gradient −2 and passes through the origin, so g(x) = −2x. (b) A line perpendicular to gradient −2 has gradient 1/2. Using (−1, 2), h(x) − 2 = (1/2)(x + 1), hence h(x) = x/2 + 5/2. (c) h(0) = 5/2, so (g ∘ h)(0) = g(5/2) = −5.

questions.summary: Determine independent, minimum, and maximum possible intersection probabilities.

6. [Maximum mark: 6]

Events A and B are such that P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.8.

(a) Determine the value of P(A ∩ B) in the case where the events A and B are independent. [1]

(b) Determine the minimum possible value of P(A ∩ B). [3]

(c) Determine the maximum possible value of P(A ∩ B), justifying your answer. [2]
questions.solution: (a) For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.3(0.8) = 0.24. (b) Since P(A ∪ B) = 1.1 − P(A ∩ B) ≤ 1, P(A ∩ B) ≥ 0.1; this minimum occurs when A ∪ B is the whole sample space. (c) An intersection cannot exceed the probability of the smaller event, so P(A ∩ B) ≤ 0.3. This maximum is attained when A ⊆ B.

questions.summary: Determine quadratic equations and ranges, then prove a quadratic and line always intersect twice using a discriminant.
questions.accessibleText:
7. [Maximum mark: 16]

(a) The graph of a quadratic function f has its vertex at the point (3, 2) and it intersects the x-axis at x = 5. Find f in the form f(x) = a(x − h)² + k. [3]

The quadratic function g is defined by g(x) = px² + (t − 1)x − p where x ∈ ℝ and p, t ∈ ℝ, p ≠ 0.

(b) In the case where g(−3) = g(1) = 4,
    (i) find the value of p and the value of t;
    (ii) find the range of g. [7]

(c) The linear function j is defined by j(x) = −x + 3p where x ∈ ℝ and p ∈ ℝ, p ≠ 0.

Show that the graphs of j(x) = −x + 3p and g(x) = px² + (t − 1)x − p have two distinct points of intersection for every possible value of p and t. [6]
questions.solution: (a) The vertex form is f(x) = a(x − 3)² + 2. Since f(5) = 0, 4a + 2 = 0, so f(x) = −(1/2)(x − 3)² + 2. (b)(i) From g(1) = 4, t − 1 = 4, so t = 5. Then g(−3) = 9p − 12 − p = 4, giving p = 2. Thus g(x) = 2x² + 4x − 2 = 2(x + 1)² − 4. (ii) Its range is [−4, ∞). (c) Equating g and j gives px² + tx − 4p = 0. Its discriminant is Δ = t² + 16p², which is strictly positive because p ≠ 0. Therefore the equation has two distinct real roots, so the graphs have two distinct intersection points for every allowed p and t.

(b) It is given that log_(ab)a = 3, where a, b ∈ ℝ⁺, ab ≠ 1.
    (i) Show that log_(ab)b = −2.
    (ii) Hence find the value of log_(ab)(∛a/√b). [8]

    (ii) Hence find the coordinates of the points on the graph of y = f(x) where f′(x) = 0. [7]

7. [Maximum mark: 16]

A particle moves in a straight line. Its displacement, s metres, from a fixed point P at time t seconds is given by s(t) = 3(t + 2)^(cos t), for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6.8, as shown in the following graph.

[Diagram: A graph of positive displacement s against time t from 0 to 6.8. The curve begins above the t-axis, rises to a small local maximum, falls to a shallow positive local minimum, then rises steeply to a much higher local maximum before falling by t = 6.8.]

(a) Find the particle’s initial displacement from the point P. [2]

(b) Find the particle’s velocity when t = 2. [2]

(c) Determine the intervals of time when the particle is moving away from the point P. [5]

The acceleration of the particle is zero when t = b and t = c, where b < c.

(d) Find the value of b and the value of c. [4]

(e) Find the total distance travelled by the particle for b ≤ t ≤ c. [3]
questions.solution: Write s(t) = 3e^[cos t·ln(t + 2)]. Then s′(t) = s(t)[−sin t·ln(t + 2) + cos t/(t + 2)]. (a) s(0) = 3(2) = 6 m. (b) s′(2) = −2.29920… = −2.30 m s⁻¹. (c) The graph stays above s = 0, so the particle moves away from P when s′(t) > 0. Solving s′(t) = 0 gives t = 0.433007…, 3.25575… and 6.33965…. Hence it moves away for 0 ≤ t < 0.433 and 3.26 < t < 6.34. (d) Solving s″(t) = 0 gives b = 1.23140… = 1.23 and c = 5.68959… = 5.69. (e) Between b and c the displacement reaches a minimum at t = 3.25575…. Thus the distance is [s(b) − s(3.25575…)] + [s(c) − s(3.25575…)] = (4.43306… − 0.577001…) + (16.2734… − 0.577001…) = 19.5525… = 19.6 m.

A circle with centre O and radius r is inscribed in sector ABC.

AB and AC are both tangent to the circle at points D and E respectively.

[Diagram not to scale: Sector ABC has vertex and centre A, straight radii AB and AC, and angle 2α at A. A circle of centre O and radius r is inscribed in the sector, tangent to AB at D, to AC at E, and internally tangent to arc BC. Radius OE is perpendicular to AC.]

R represents the shaded region shown in the following diagram.

[Diagram not to scale: The same sector and inscribed circle. Region R is the part of quadrilateral ADOE between A and the minor circular arc ED; it is bounded by tangent segments AE and AD and the circle's minor arc from E to D.]

(b) (i) Find ∠DOE in terms of α.
    (ii) Hence or otherwise, find an expression for the area of R. [5]

(c) Find the value of α for which the area of R is equal to the area of the circle of centre O and radius r. [4]
questions.solution: (a) In right triangle AOE, ∠EAO = α and OE = r, so AE = r/tanα. Quadrilateral ADOE consists of two congruent right triangles, hence its area is 2·(1/2)·r·(r/tanα) = r²/tanα. (b)(i) Since ∠AEO = ∠ADO = π/2 and ∠EAD = 2α, the angle sum in ADOE gives ∠DOE = π − 2α. (ii) Region R is the quadrilateral minus sector DOE, so area(R) = r²/tanα − (1/2)r²(π − 2α). (c) Set this equal to πr² and cancel r²: 1/tanα − (1/2)(π − 2α) = π. Solving for 0 < α < π/2 gives α = 0.218979… = 0.219 radians.

9. [Maximum mark: 16]

The time worked, T, in hours per week by employees of a large company is normally distributed with a mean of 42 and standard deviation 10.7.

(a) Find the probability that an employee selected at random works more than 40 hours per week. [2]

(b) A group of four employees is selected at random. Each employee is asked in turn whether they work more than 40 hours per week. Find the probability that the fourth employee is the only one in the group who works more than 40 hours per week. [3]

(c) A large group of employees work more than 40 hours per week.
    (i) An employee is selected at random from this large group. Find the probability that this employee works less than 55 hours per week.
    (ii) Ten employees are selected at random from this large group. Find the probability that exactly five of them work less than 55 hours per week. [7]

It is known that P(a ≤ T ≤ b) = 0.904 and that P(T > b) = 2P(T < a), where a and b are numbers of hours worked per week. An employee who works fewer than a hours per week is considered to be a part-time employee.

(d) Find the maximum time, in hours per week, that an employee can work and still be considered part-time. [4]
questions.solution: Let T ~ N(42, 10.7²). (a) P(T > 40) = 0.574136… = 0.574. (b) The first three must work at most 40 hours and the fourth more than 40, so the probability is (1 − 0.574136…)³(0.574136…) = 0.0443430… = 0.0443. (c)(i) P(T < 55 | T > 40) = P(40 < T < 55)/P(T > 40) = 0.804590… = 0.805. (ii) If X ~ B(10, 0.804590…), then P(X = 5) = C(10,5)(0.804590…)⁵(1 − 0.804590…)⁵ = 0.0242111… = 0.0242. (d) Let x = P(T < a). Since P(T > b) = 2x, x + 0.904 + 2x = 1, so x = 0.032. The normal quantile satisfying P(T < a) = 0.032 is a = 22.18167…, giving a maximum part-time threshold of 22.2 hours per week.
